The Brain & Nervous System

Your body's command center and the lightning-fast messenger network that connects every part of you.

Chapter 1 · The Big Idea

Imagine a City Without Communication

Think about a giant city. It has a mayor who makes decisions, roads connecting every neighborhood, and phones and computers sending messages everywhere. Your body works in a surprisingly similar way.

The mayor is your brain. The highway is your spinal cord. The roads and cables are your nerves.

The brain is the mayor and command center. The spinal cord is the main highway. The nerves are the roads and communication cables. And the neurons are the messengers carrying information.

Together, they form the nervous system, one of the most important systems in your body. It helps you think, learn, remember, move, feel, breathe, and even keeps your heart beating while you sleep.

Chapter 2 · The Network

What Is the Nervous System?

The nervous system is your body's communication network. It constantly gathers information from inside and outside your body, processes that information, and sends instructions about what to do next.

Three jobs, over and over: gather information, process it, then decide what to do. Your nervous system does this thousands of times every single second, even right now as you read.

Watch it work

Every one of these everyday moments runs through your nervous system:

🔥 Hot stove

You touch it, then pull your hand away before you even think.

📣 Your name

You hear it across a room and turn your head toward the sound.

🍪 Cookies

You smell them baking and suddenly feel hungry.

➕ Math

You solve a problem using memory and reasoning.

Quick Check
Which three jobs does the nervous system do over and over?
Chapter 3 · Two Main Parts

The CNS and the PNS

Scientists split the nervous system into two teams that work together: the central team in the middle, and the peripheral team reaching everywhere else.

Pink = central (brain and spinal cord). Yellow = peripheral (nerves everywhere else).
Reference Diagram
The peripheral nervous system (yellow) branches out from the brain and spinal cord (pink).
Reference Diagram
The central nervous system: the brain and spinal cord, shown in cross section.

1. Central Nervous System

The headquarters. It receives information and makes the decisions.

  • The brain: the control center for memory, movement, emotion, and learning
  • The spinal cord: the superhighway carrying messages up and down

2. Peripheral Nervous System

All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, branching like the roots of a tree.

  • Connects to arms, legs, skin, eyes, and ears
  • Connects to muscles and internal organs
  • Without it, the brain would not know what is happening in the body
🧠 Pause and Think
If a doctor says "the central nervous system," which two body parts are they talking about?
The brain and the spinal cord. These two together form the headquarters. Every nerve outside of them belongs to the peripheral nervous system instead.
Chapter 4 · The Messenger Cell

Meet the Neuron

The basic working unit of the nervous system is the neuron. Neurons are specialized cells that send messages throughout the body. Every thought, movement, memory, and sensation depends on them. Scientists estimate the human brain contains tens of billions of neurons.

A signal pulse races from the cell body, down the axon, to the terminals. Some axons stretch from your spinal cord all the way to your foot.

A neuron has three main parts. The dendrites are like antennae that receive incoming messages. The cell body is the control center that processes information and keeps the cell alive. The axon is a long extension that carries messages away from the cell body.

Reference Diagram
Every labeled part: dendrites, nucleus, cell body, axon, the myelin sheath that insulates it, and the axon terminals at the synapse.
Real Microscope Image
An actual neuron stained and viewed under a microscope. You can see the cell body, nucleus, and nucleolus.

Chapter 5 · Sending Messages

Electricity Meets Chemistry

Neurons send messages using both electrical signals and chemical signals. This combination makes communication incredibly fast. Imagine touching a hot pan:

All five steps happen in a fraction of a second.
🧠 Pause and Think
Why is it useful that this whole sequence happens so quickly?
Speed protects you. The faster the signal travels, the faster you can move away from danger like heat or a sharp object, which means less time for your body to get hurt.
Chapter 6 · The Tiny Gap

Synapses: Where Neurons Talk

Here is something surprising: neurons usually do not physically touch each other. Instead, there is a tiny gap called a synapse. When a signal reaches the end of one neuron, chemicals called neurotransmitters cross the gap and deliver the message to the next neuron.

Think of neurotransmitters as tiny mail carriers, swimming across the gap to deliver each message.
Reference Illustration
A close-up of the synapse. Neurotransmitter chemicals are packed in little bubbles, then released into the gap to reach the next neuron.
Quick Check
What carries the message across the synapse gap between two neurons?
Chapter 7 · Three Specialists

Three Types of Neurons

Not all neurons do the same job. There are three kinds, each with its own role on the team.

👀 Sensory Neurons

These collect information from the world through sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. They send information toward the brain and spinal cord.

💪 Motor Neurons

These carry instructions from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles. They help you walk, jump, smile, throw a ball, and speak.

🔗 Interneurons

These connect neurons to other neurons. They help process information and make decisions. Most neurons in the brain are interneurons.

An easy way to remember: Sensory neurons bring news IN. Motor neurons send orders OUT. Interneurons are the thinkers in the MIDDLE that connect everything.
🧠 Pause and Think
You decide to wave hello to a friend. Which type of neuron sends the command to your arm muscles?
Motor neurons. They carry the instruction out from your brain and spinal cord to the muscles in your arm so they can move and wave.
Chapter 8 · Inside the Brain

The Brain's Major Regions

Your brain is not one single blob. It has different regions, and each one has a special job. Tap a region below to light it up.

TAP A REGION

Tap the cerebrum, cerebellum, or brainstem above to learn what each part controls.

Cerebrum

The largest part of the brain. It is responsible for thinking, learning, language, memory, problem solving, and voluntary movement. This is the wrinkly part most people picture when they imagine a brain.

Cerebellum

Located near the back of the brain, the cerebellum handles balance, coordination, and fine movement. It helps you ride a bicycle, catch a ball, or play a musical instrument.

Brainstem

The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord. It controls automatic functions such as breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, and sleeping and waking. You never have to think about these because the brainstem handles them for you.

Reference Diagram
The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord. Its parts include the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.
Real Anatomical View
A detailed anatomical drawing of the brain sliced down the middle. You can spot the cerebellum, pons, medulla, and spinal cord.

Chapter 9 · Emergency Speed

Reflexes: Faster Than Thought

Sometimes your body reacts before your brain fully processes what happened. These quick reactions are called reflexes. When you touch something hot, your hand moves away almost instantly. The spinal cord can coordinate this response before the brain even becomes fully aware. This helps protect you from injury.

The signal can loop through the spinal cord and back out before your brain has even caught up.
Reference Diagram
The five steps of a reflex arc: receptors detect the hot stimulus, a sensory neuron carries it in, an interneuron relays it, a motor neuron carries the command out, and the muscles move the hand away.
Reference Diagram
The full reflex arc through the skin, sensory neuron, spinal cord, and motor neuron back to the muscle.
Reference Diagram
A closer look: the signal comes in (afferent) through the dorsal root and goes out (efferent) through the ventral root.
🧠 Pause and Think
A reflex skips a step that normal decisions use. What step does it skip to save time?
It does not wait for the brain to fully think it over. The spinal cord handles the response directly, so your hand moves before your brain has even finished understanding what happened.
Chapter 10 · Choosing vs Automatic

Voluntary and Involuntary Actions

✂ Voluntary Actions

Actions you choose to do, using conscious control.

  • Writing
  • Running
  • Talking
  • Playing sports

♻ Involuntary Actions

Actions your body does automatically, even while you sleep.

  • Breathing
  • Digesting food
  • Sweating
  • Heartbeat
Quick Check
Which of these is an INVOLUNTARY action?
Chapter 11 · Gathering Tools

The Nervous System and Your Five Senses

Your senses are information-gathering tools. Sensory neurons send everything they collect to the brain, where it is turned into the world you experience.

👀

Eyes collect light.

👂

Ears collect sound vibrations.

👃

Nose detects chemicals in the air.

👅

Tongue detects chemicals in food.

✋

Skin detects pressure, temperature, and pain.

Reference Diagram
Signals from the face, arm, trunk, and leg travel up the spinal cord, pass through the thalamus, and reach the sensory cortex.
Reference Diagram
Different kinds of feeling, like gentle touch versus sharp pain, travel to the brain along different pathways.
Chapter 12 · Growing & Resting

Memory, Learning, and Sleep

How learning changes your brain

Every time you learn something new, neurons strengthen existing connections or form brand new pathways. Scientists describe these neural pathways as information highways connecting different parts of the brain. Learning multiplication facts, practicing piano, or getting better at basketball all involve changes in these connections.

Sleep is not "off"

Sleep does not turn the brain off. While you sleep, your brain stays active. Research suggests sleep helps organize memories, process information, support learning, and keep your brain healthy.

Reference Chart
Your brain produces different waves at different times. Fast gamma and beta waves mean an active, busy mind, while slow theta and delta waves appear during drowsiness and deep sleep.
🧠 Pause and Think
Why might practicing a piano piece a little every day work better than practicing once for many hours?
Each practice session strengthens the neural pathways for that skill, and sleep in between helps organize and lock in what you learned. Spacing practice out gives your brain repeated chances to build stronger connections.
Chapter 13 · When Things Break

What Happens If the Nervous System Is Damaged?

Because the nervous system controls so much, damage can cause many different problems. The exact effect depends on where the injury happens. Depending on the location, a person might have trouble moving, speaking, learning, remembering, feeling sensations, or keeping their balance.

Connecting the dots: If balance is the cerebellum's job, then an injury there might affect balance. If breathing is the brainstem's job, an injury there is far more serious. The location of the damage points to the function that is lost.
Real Medical Scan
An MRI lets doctors look inside the brain without surgery. Scans like these help find exactly where an injury is located.
Chapter 14 · Amazing Truths

Fun Facts to Remember

1

Your nervous system runs on electrical signals.

2

Your brain contains tens of billions of neurons.

3

Every thought you have depends on neurons communicating.

4

Some axons can stretch nearly a meter long.

5

The brain keeps working the entire time you sleep.

6

Reflexes can happen faster than conscious thought.

7

Brain plus spinal cord equals the central nervous system.

8

The nerves throughout your body form the peripheral nervous system.
